::: {#prop:3.1 .proposition}
**Proposition 3.1** (3.1). *On a two-dimensional smooth compact
connected manifold with boundary, not homeomorphic to the disc $D^2$,
there exists an exact function with two critical points.*
:::

*Proof.* Any two-dimensional compact connected manifold with boundary
admits a filtration by two manifolds with boundary
$$M_1 \subset M_2 = M,$$ satisfying the hypotheses of
Theorem [2.6](#thm:2.5){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:2.5"}. This
follows from the covering of the manifold by two discs (Fig. 1.3). By
Proposition [1.12](#prop:1.10){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:1.10"} and
Theorem [2.13](#thm:2.12){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:2.12"},
the constructed function is exact. 0◻

We now consider the second type of $P$-functions --- round functions.

::: {#thm:3.2 .theorem}
**Theorem 3.2** (3.2). *On a manifold homeomorphic to the sphere $S^2$,
to the projective plane $\mathbb{R}P^2$, or to the disc $D^2$, there
exist no round functions. On every other two-dimensional smooth compact
connected manifold round functions exist.*
:::

*Proof.* Suppose a round function $f$ exists on the sphere $S^2$. By
compactness of $S^2$, the number of its critical circles is finite. Take
any critical value $c$ of $f$ and a neighbourhood
$(c - \varepsilon, c + \varepsilon)$ for some $\varepsilon > 0$ such
that no other critical value lies in
$[c - \varepsilon, c + \varepsilon]$. The critical value $c$ corresponds
to a finite number of critical circles. Remove from $S^2$ the critical
layer $$f^{-1}[c - \varepsilon, c + \varepsilon] = M_c.$$ By Jordan's
theorem the closure of the remaining set is a disjoint union of
submanifolds $D_1$ and $D_2$:
$$\overline{S^2 \setminus f^{-1}[c - \varepsilon, c + \varepsilon]} = D_1 \cup D_2,$$
each with a single boundary component
$$\partial D_1 = f^{-1}(c - \varepsilon)\quad\text{and}\quad
   \partial D_2 = f^{-1}(c + \varepsilon).$$ Suppose that in one of
these submanifolds, say $D_1$, there are no critical points of $f$. Then
$D_1$ must be homeomorphic to $$\partial D_1 \times I,$$ that is, to a
manifold with two boundary components. This contradiction shows that
$D_1$ and $D_2$ must contain critical circles.

Take the next critical value $b$ of $f$ (say $b > c$) such that $(c, b)$
contains no critical values, and $\delta > 0$ small enough that
$(b, b + \delta)$ also contains no critical values. The value $b$
corresponds to finitely many critical circles. Removing the layer
$f^{-1}[c + \varepsilon, b + \delta] = M_b$ from $D_2$, we obtain
$$D_3 = \overline{D_2 \setminus M_b}.$$ Since $D_3$ has only one
boundary component $\partial D_3 = f^{-1}(b + \delta)$, $D_3$ must also
contain critical circles. Continuing in this way to remove critical
layers we exhaust the set of critical values. But the remaining
submanifold will have a single boundary component and therefore must
contain critical points. This contradiction shows that no round function
exists on a manifold homeomorphic to $S^2$. Analogous arguments for
manifolds homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}P^2$ or to $D^2$ show that no round
functions exist on these manifolds either.

On every two-dimensional smooth compact connected manifold without
boundary, other than $S^2$ and $\mathbb{R}P^2$, round functions exist.
This is visually clear from the example of the height function.
Figure 3.2 displays a manifold homeomorphic to a sphere with three
handles, on which the height function has six critical circles.

A round function on a manifold without boundary can also be defined by
its level lines. For this, represent the manifold as a fundamental
polygon $W$ in the symmetric canonical form
$$W = a_1\ldots a_n a_1^{-1}\ldots a_{n-1}^{-1} a_n^{\,e},$$ where
$e = -1$ corresponds to the orientable case and $e = 1$ to the
non-orientable one, and transfer the level lines (say, of the height
function) onto the fundamental polygon. Figure 3.3 shows level lines of
a round function on the double torus.

<figure id="fig:3.3" data-latex-placement="h">

<figcaption aria-hidden="true"></figcaption>
</figure>

On a non-orientable manifold a round function can also be given by its
level lines. Suppose the non-orientable manifold has the symmetric
canonical form $$W = a_1\ldots a_n a_1^{-1}\ldots a_{n-1}^{-1} a_n.$$
Define the level lines of a round function on the corresponding
orientable manifold
$$W = a_1\ldots a_n a_1^{-1}\ldots a_{n-1}^{-1} a_n^{-1}$$ so that the
side $a_n$ of the fundamental polygon corresponds to one of the critical
circles on the manifold. These level lines will also be level lines of a
round function on the corresponding non-orientable manifold.

On a manifold with boundary we define a round function via its level
lines as follows. Recall that on manifolds with boundary we consider
only functions taking a constant maximal value on the boundary and
having no critical points there. Adjoin to $M$ (with boundary
$\partial M$) a manifold $N$ with boundary homeomorphic to $\partial M$,
so that the "glued" manifold has no boundary. One may take $N = M$
(Fig. 3.4).

On the fundamental polygon of the "glued" manifold without boundary,
define the round function via its level lines as above. Cut the polygon
along the level lines forming the boundary of $M$ and remove from the
polygon the part corresponding to the adjoined piece $N$. The remaining
level lines give a round function on the manifold with boundary.

::: {#thm:3.3 .theorem}
**Theorem 3.3** (3.3). *On every two-dimensional smooth compact
connected manifold not homeomorphic to the disc $D^2$, the sphere $S^2$
or the projective plane $\mathbb{R}P^2$, there exists an exact round
function whose number of singularities equals:*

1.  *two on the torus and the Klein bottle;*

2.  *three on the remaining manifolds without boundary;*

3.  *one on the annulus $S^1 \times I$ and on the Möbius band;*

4.  *two on the remaining manifolds with boundary.*
:::

*Proof.* Let the torus be given by
$$T^2 = S^1 \times S^1 = \{(x_1, \ldots, x_4) \in \mathbb{R}^4 :\;
      x_1^2 + x_2^2 = 1,\; x_3^2 + x_4^2 = 1\}.$$ The restriction of
$f = x_1$ to $S^1 \times S^1$ is an exact function with two critical
circles.

The Klein bottle is obtained from the torus by cutting along the circle
$$\{(x_1, \ldots, x_4) \in \mathbb{R}^4 :\; x_1 = 0,\; x_2 = 1,\; x_3^2 + x_4^2 = 1\}$$
and identifying the boundaries via
$$(0, 1, x_3, x_4) \mapsto (0, 1, x_3, -x_4).$$ The function $f = x_1$,
restricted to the Klein bottle, is exact and has two critical circles.

On the remaining manifolds without boundary an exact function is defined
by its smooth level lines (the function is naturally not uniquely
determined). Since such a manifold can be covered by three closed sets
$Q_1$, $Q_2$, $Q_3$ intersecting pairwise along finitely many arcs
(Proposition [1.13](#prop:1.11){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:1.11"}), each homeomorphic to the annulus
$S^1 \times I$, take as level surfaces in $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ the circles
$$S^1 \times t_0,\quad\text{where } t_0 \in I.$$ Extending in $Q_3$
neighbourhoods of the intersection arcs $Q_1 \cap Q_3$ and
$Q_2 \cap Q_3$ so that those arcs lie on the circle in $Q_3$
$$S^1 \times t_0,\quad t_0 = 0.5,$$ we obtain a system of level lines
for a function on the manifold.

On the annulus $S^1 \times I$ given by
$$\{(x_1, x_2, x_3) \in \mathbb{R}^3 :\; x_1^2 + x_2^2 = 1,\; 0 \leq x_3 \leq 1\},$$
the function $$f = (x_3 - 0.5)^2$$ with one critical circle is exact.

The Möbius band is obtained from $S^1 \times I$ by cutting along
$$\{(x_1, x_2, x_3) \in \mathbb{R}^3 :\; x_1 = 0,\; x_2 = 1,\; 0 \leq x_3 \leq 1\}$$
and identifying the boundaries via $$(0, 1, x_3) \mapsto (0, 1, -x_3).$$
The function $$f = (x_3 - 0.5)^2$$ with one critical circle is exact.

On the remaining manifolds with boundary one may define a round function
via its smooth level lines analogously to what was done for manifolds
without boundary. 0◻

### $P$-functions on three-dimensional manifolds

::: {#thm:3.4 .theorem}
**Theorem 3.4** (3.4). *On every three-dimensional smooth compact
connected manifold without boundary a round function exists. If the
manifold is homeomorphic to one of*

1.  *the sphere $S^3$,*

2.  *the projective space $\mathbb{R}P^3$,*

3.  *the manifold $S^1 \times S^2$,*

4.  *a lens space,*

*then it admits an exact round function with two critical circles. If
the manifold is homeomorphic to the torus $T^3$, then it admits an exact
round function with three critical circles. On every other
three-dimensional smooth compact connected manifold there exists a round
function whose number of singularities does not exceed four.*
:::

*Proof.* It is known that if a three-dimensional manifold is
homeomorphic to one of $S^3$, $\mathbb{R}P^3$, $S^1 \times S^2$, or a
lens space, then it admits a Heegaard diagram of genus one. This means
that each such manifold can be represented as the gluing of two solid
tori $$S^1 \times D^2$$ along some homeomorphism of their boundaries. If
on one of the solid tori one defines a differentiable function taking a
constant maximal value on the boundary $S^1 \times S^1$ and having one
critical circle, then the required round function is obtained by
extending it to the second solid torus by the negative of the function
plus an appropriate constant. The resulting function is exact. This
follows from the main theorem and
Proposition [1.14](#prop:1.12){reference-type="ref"
reference="prop:1.12"}.

If the three-dimensional manifold is homeomorphic to the torus $T^3$,
then by Corollary [2.17](#cor:2.16){reference-type="ref"
reference="cor:2.16"} there exists on it an exact round function with
three critical circles.

Every other three-dimensional smooth compact connected manifold $M$
without boundary admits a Heegaard diagram of genus $g \geq 2$. This
means that $M$ may be presented as the gluing of two handlebodies $M_1$
and $M_2$ with $g$ handles each, where each handle $$D^2 \times I$$ is
attached to the ball along the set $$D^2 \times S^0.$$ Cut each of the
handlebodies along $g$ handles into two parts so that each is
homeomorphic to $$S^1 \times D^2$$ (Fig. 1.8). Denote these parts by
$N_i$, $i = 1, \ldots, 4$, so that
$$M_1 = N_1 \cup N_2,\quad M_2 = N_3 \cup N_4.$$ Define on $M_1$ a
differentiable function $f$ taking a constant maximal value $a$ on
$\partial M_1$ and having two critical circles. This can be done, for
instance, as in Theorem [2.6](#thm:2.5){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:2.5"}, by taking an appropriate filtration of $M_1$.

The function $F\colon M \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by
$$F = \begin{cases} f(x), & \text{if } x \in M_1,\\
      2a - f(x), & \text{if } x \in M_2,\end{cases}$$ is the required
one. 0◻

### $P$-functions on $n$-dimensional manifolds

::: {#thm:3.5 .theorem}
**Theorem 3.5** (3.5). *Let $P = S^{n-1}$ be the $(n-1)$-dimensional
sphere. Then on the $n$-dimensional sphere there are no $P$-functions.*
:::

*Proof.* Suppose an $S^{n-1}$-function $f$ exists on $S^n$. Take any of
its values $a$ and the corresponding critical submanifold --- a sphere
$S_1^{n-1}$.

By the Jordan--Brouwer theorem, every $(n-1)$-dimensional submanifold of
$\mathbb{R}^n$ homeomorphic to a sphere divides the ambient space into
two components and is their common boundary. If from $S^n$ we remove a
sufficiently small cylindrical neighbourhood $C_\varepsilon(S_1^{n-1})$
of the critical sphere $S_1^{n-1}$, we obtain a disjoint union of two
connected components $D_1$ and $D_2$ with boundaries
$$\partial D_1 = f^{-1}(a - \varepsilon)\quad\text{and}\quad
   \partial D_2 = f^{-1}(a + \varepsilon)$$ respectively (for
sufficiently small $\varepsilon > 0$).

The submanifold $D_1$ must contain critical points; otherwise it would
be homeomorphic to $$\partial D_1 \times I,$$ that is, to a manifold
with two boundary components. Let the critical sphere $S_2^{n-1}$ in
$D_1$ correspond to a critical value $b < a$ such that $(b, a)$ contains
no critical values. Removing from $D_1$ the subset
$$f^{-1}(a - \varepsilon, b + \delta)\cup C_\varepsilon(S_2^{n-1})$$ for
small $\delta > 0$, we obtain a submanifold $D_1'$ with single boundary
component $$\partial D_1' = f^{-1}(b - \delta),$$ which must again
contain critical points. Continuing in this way to remove critical
layers we exhaust the supply of critical submanifolds, which is finite
by compactness of $S^n$. A submanifold with single boundary component
remains, in which there must be no critical points. This contradiction
completes the proof. 0◻

::: {#thm:3.6 .theorem}
**Theorem 3.6** (3.6). *Let $P = S^1$ be the one-dimensional sphere, and
let $n \geq 3$. Then on the $n$-dimensional sphere there exists a
$P$-function whose number of singularities does not exceed
$$[n/2] + 1.$$*
:::

*Proof.* By Theorem [3.4](#thm:3.4){reference-type="ref"
reference="thm:3.4"}, on the three-dimensional sphere there exists a
round function with two singularities.

Consider the four-dimensional sphere $S^4$. Realize it as the quotient
$$S^4 = D^4 / S^3.$$ Let the disc $D^4$ be given by
$$D^4 = \{(x_1, \ldots, x_4) \in \mathbb{R}^4 :\; x_i^2 \leq 1,\; i = 1, \ldots, 4\}.$$
Consider three subsets of the disc: $$\begin{align*}
N_1 &= \{(x_1, \ldots, x_4) \in \mathbb{R}^4 :\; x_1^2 \leq 1,\; x_i^2 \leq \varepsilon,\; i = 2, 3, 4\},\\ N_2 &= \{(x_1, \ldots, x_4) \in \mathbb{R}^4 :\; 1 - \varepsilon \leq x_i^2 \leq 1,\; i = 1, \ldots, 4\},\\ N_3 &= \overline{D^4 \setminus (N_1 \cup N_2)}\\ &= \{(x_1, \ldots, x_4) \in \mathbb{R}^4 :\; x_1^2 \leq 1 - \varepsilon,\; \varepsilon \leq x_i^2 \leq 1 - \varepsilon,\; i = 2, 3, 4\}
\end{align*}$$ for sufficiently small $\varepsilon > 0$. Cover $S^4$ by
two subsets $M_1$ and $M_2$, the images of $N_1 \cup N_2$ and $N_3$
under the quotient. $M_1$ is homeomorphic to $$S^1 \times D^3,$$ and
$M_2$ is homeomorphic to $$S^2 \times D^2.$$ $M_2$ can be covered by two
subsets with disjoint interiors, each homeomorphic to
$$S^1 \times D^3.$$ Together with $M_1$, these subsets cover $S^4$.
After smoothing corners where needed and taking an appropriate
filtration of the sphere, we are in the situation of
Theorem [2.6](#thm:2.5){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:2.5"},
whence the existence of a round function with three critical circles on
the four-dimensional sphere follows.

The five-dimensional sphere is covered analogously by two subsets
$$M_1 = S^1 \times D^4\quad\text{and}\quad M_2 = S^3 \times D^2.$$ The
sphere $S^3$, and hence $M_2$, admits a covering by two subsets with
disjoint interiors, each homeomorphic to $$S^1 \times D^4.$$ By
Theorem [2.6](#thm:2.5){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:2.5"}, on
the five-dimensional sphere there exists a round function with three
critical circles.

It is not difficult to see that an analogous treatment of
higher-dimensional spheres yields the statement of the theorem. 0◻

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#def:1.1 .definition} **Definition 1.1** (1.1). Let $A$, $B$, $P$ be closed subsets of a Hausdorff topological space, with $P \subset B$ and $A \subset B$. The *$P$-category* $\mathop{\mathrm{P\text{-}cat}}_B A$ of the set $A$ relative to the set $B$ is the minimal number $k$ of closed subsets $A_1, \ldots, A_k$ in $B$ that satisfy the following properties: 1. $A$ is their union $$A = \bigcup_{i=1}^{k} A_i;$$ 2. each subset $A_i$ is contractible within $B$ to $P$. :::
nodes.statement: Definition 1.1 (1.1). Let $A$, $B$, $P$ be closed subsets of a Hausdorff topological space, with $P \subset B$ and $A \subset B$. The $P$-category $\mathop{\mathrm{P\text{-}cat}}_B A$ of the set $A$ relative to the set $B$ is the minimal number $k$ of closed subsets $A_1, \ldots, A_k$ in $B$ that satisfy the following properties: 1. $A$ is their union $A = \bigcup_{i=1}^{k} A_i$; 2. each subset $A_i$, $i=1,\ldots,k$, is contractible within $B$ to $P$. That is, for each subset $A_i$ there exists a homotopy $F_i\colon A_i \times I \to B$ such that $F_i(x,0) = x$, $x \in A_i$; $F_i(x,t) \in B$, $x \in A_i$, $0 < t < 1$; $F_i(x,1) = P_i \subset B$, where $P_i$ is homeomorphic to $P$. If no such number $k$ exists, we set $\mathop{\mathrm{P\text{-}cat}}_B A = \infty$. The subsets $A_1, \ldots, A_k$ are called categorical. The $P$-category of a set $A$ relative to itself is simply called the $P$-category of $A$ and denoted $\mathop{\mathrm{P\text{-}cat}}A$. If $A$ coincides with the whole topological space, then $\mathop{\mathrm{P\text{-}cat}}A$ denotes the $P$-category of that space.

Let $H^*(M; A)$ be the cohomology ring of $M$ ... Consider all integers $q$ such that in $H^*(M; A)$ there exist elements $a_1, \ldots, a_q$ satisfying: 1. $\dim a_i > 0$; 2. $a_1 \cdots a_q$ is non-zero; 3. $\dim (a_1 \cdots a_q) \leq m - p$. The *cohomological $p$-length* of $M$ is the largest such number $q$. :::
nodes.statement: Definition 1.4 (1.3). Let $m$ be the dimension of a manifold $M$ and let $p$ be a non-negative integer. Let $H^*(M; A)$ be the cohomology ring of $M$, where $A = \mathbb{Z}$ or $\mathbb{R}$ when $M$ is orientable, and $A = \mathbb{Z}_2$ when $M$ is non-orientable. Consider all integers $q$ such that in the cohomology ring $H^*(M; A)$ there exist elements $a_1, \ldots, a_q$ satisfying: 1. $\dim a_i > 0$, $i = 1, \ldots, q$; 2. the product $a_1 \cdots a_q$ (with respect to the multiplication in $H^*(M; A)$) is non-zero; 3. $\dim (a_1 \cdots a_q) \leq m - p$. The cohomological $p$-length of $M$ is the largest such number $q$.

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#def:1.3prime .definition} **Definition 1.5** (1.3$'$). With the notation of Definition 1.4, the *homological $p$-length* of $M$ is the largest number $q$ of cycles $c_1, \ldots, c_q$ of $M$ satisfying: 1. $\dim c_i < m$; 2. $\bigcap_{i=1}^{q} c_i = c$ is a cycle not homologous to zero; 3. $\dim c \geq p$. :::
nodes.statement: Definition 1.5 (1.3'). With the notation of Definition 1.4, the homological $p$-length of $M$ is the largest number $q$ of cycles $c_1, \ldots, c_q$ of $M$ satisfying: 1. $\dim c_i < m$, $i=1,\ldots,q$; 2. $\bigcap_{i=1}^{q} c_i = c$ is a cycle not homologous to zero; 3. $\dim c \geq p$.

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#rem:1.4 .remark} **Remark 1.6** (1.4). None of the cycles $c_1, \ldots, c_q$ in the definition of $p$-length may contain another ... If $M$ has a boundary, then only absolute cycles of $M$ are considered. :::
nodes.statement: Remark 1.6 (1.4). None of the cycles $c_1, \ldots, c_q$ in the definition of $p$-length may contain another, otherwise the definition would lose meaning, since one would have to consider only manifolds of infinite length. If $M$ has a boundary, then in the definition of $p$-length only absolute cycles of $M$ are considered.

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#thm:1.5 .theorem} **Theorem 1.7** (1.5). *If $M$ is a manifold without boundary, then $$\mathop{\mathrm{P\text{-}cat}}M \;\geq\; \mathrm{long}^{\,p} M + 1.$$ If $M$ is a manifold with boundary, then $$\mathop{\mathrm{P\text{-}cat}}M \;\geq\; \mathrm{long}^{\,p} M.$$* :::
nodes.statement: Theorem 1.7 (1.5). If $M$ is a manifold without boundary, then its $P$-category is at least one more than the $p$-length of $M$: $\mathop{\mathrm{P\text{-}cat}}M \geq \mathrm{long}^{p} M + 1$. If $M$ is a manifold with boundary, then its $P$-category is at least the $p$-length of $M$: $\mathop{\mathrm{P\text{-}cat}}M \geq \mathrm{long}^{p} M$.

nodes.statement: Proposition 1.8 (1.6). Let $(N; \partial N)$ be obtained from the sphere $S^2$ by removing a finite number $s$ of open discs: $(N; \partial N) = (S^2 \setminus \bigcup_{i=1}^{s} D_i^2; \bigcup_{i=1}^{s} S_i^1)$, and let $(L; \partial L)$ be obtained from the projective plane $\mathbb{R}P^2$ by removing a finite number $k$ of open discs: $(L; \partial L) = (\mathbb{R}P^2 \setminus \bigcup_{i=1}^{k} D_i^2; \bigcup_{i=1}^{k} S_i^1)$. For $p = 0$ the $p$-length of a two-dimensional compact connected manifold equals: 1. one, if the manifold is homeomorphic to $(N; \partial N)$, to $(L; \partial L)$, or to the sphere $S^2$; 2. two, on the other manifolds. For $p = 1$ the $p$-length of a two-dimensional compact connected manifold equals: 1. zero, if the manifold is homeomorphic to the sphere $S^2$ or to the disc $D^2$; 2. one, on the other manifolds.

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#thm:1.7 .theorem} **Theorem 1.9** (1.7). *Let $M = S^{k_1} \times \ldots \times S^{k_r}$ ... Then $$\mathrm{long}^{\,p} M \;\geq\; r - \min l(p),$$ where the minimum is over subsets with $\sum k_{i_j} \geq p$.* :::
nodes.statement: Theorem 1.9 (1.7). Let $M = S^{k_1} \times S^{k_2} \times \ldots \times S^{k_r}$ be a product of $k_i$-dimensional spheres, $i = 1, \ldots, r$, and let $p$ be a non-negative integer. Then $\mathrm{long}^{p} M \geq r - \min l(p)$, where the minimum is taken over all subsets $\{(k_{i_1}, k_{i_2}, \ldots, k_{i_l}) \subset (k_1, k_2, \ldots, k_r) : \sum_{j=1}^{l} k_{i_j} \geq p\}$.

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#cor:1.8 .corollary} **Corollary 1.10** (1.8). *Let $M = S^{k_1} \times \ldots \times S^{k_r}$ ... Then $$\mathrm{long}\, M = r.$$* :::
nodes.statement: Corollary 1.10 (1.8). Let $M = S^{k_1} \times S^{k_2} \times \ldots \times S^{k_r}$ be a product of $k_i$-dimensional spheres, $i = 1, \ldots, r$. Then the (co)homological length of $M$ equals the number $r$ of factors: $\mathrm{long}\, M = r$.

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#prop:1.9 .proposition} **Proposition 1.11** (1.9). *The $p$-length of the $n$-dimensional torus is $p$ less than its dimension: $$\mathrm{long}^{\,p} T^n = n - p.$$* :::
nodes.statement: Proposition 1.11 (1.9). The $p$-length of the $n$-dimensional torus is $p$ less than its dimension: $\mathrm{long}^{p} T^n = n - p$.

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#prop:1.10 .proposition} **Proposition 1.12** (1.10). *The Lyusternik--Shnirelman category of a 2-dim compact connected manifold with boundary, not homeomorphic to $D^2$, equals two. Moreover, the categorical sets may intersect only along their boundaries, each homeomorphic to $D^2$.* :::
nodes.statement: Proposition 1.12 (1.10). The Lyusternik--Shnirelman category of a two-dimensional compact connected manifold with boundary, not homeomorphic to the disc $D^2$, equals two. Moreover, the categorical sets may be chosen so as to intersect only along their boundaries, and so that each is homeomorphic to the disc $D^2$.

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#prop:1.11 .proposition} **Proposition 1.13** (1.11). *The round category of a 2-dim compact connected manifold equals: 1. one if ~= $S^1 \times I$ or Möbius band; 2. two on remaining manifolds with boundary; 3. two if ~= $S^2$, $\mathbb{R}P^2$, $T^2$ or Klein bottle; 4. three on remaining manifolds without boundary.* :::
nodes.statement: Proposition 1.13 (1.11). The round category of a two-dimensional compact connected manifold equals: 1. one, if the manifold is homeomorphic to $S^1 \times I$ or to the Möbius band; 2. two, on the remaining manifolds with boundary; 3. two, if the manifold is homeomorphic to the sphere $S^2$, the projective plane $\mathbb{R}P^2$, the torus $T^2$ or the Klein bottle; 4. three, on the remaining manifolds without boundary.

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#prop:1.12 .proposition} **Proposition 1.14** (1.12). *The round category of a 3-dim compact connected manifold without boundary: 1. equals two if ~= $S^3$, $S^1 \times S^2$, $\mathbb{R}P^3$, or a lens space; 2. equals three on $T^3$; 3. does not exceed four on the remaining manifolds.* :::
nodes.statement: Proposition 1.14 (1.12). The round category of a three-dimensional compact connected manifold without boundary 1. equals two if the manifold is homeomorphic to one of the following: the sphere $S^3$; $S^1 \times S^2$; the projective space $\mathbb{R}P^3$; a lens space obtainable as a quotient of $S^3$ by a differentiable action of the group $\mathbb{Z}_p$; 2. equals three on the torus $T^3$; 3. does not exceed four on the remaining manifolds.

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#thm:1.13 .theorem} **Theorem 1.15** (1.13). *Let $M = S^{k_1} \times \ldots \times S^{k_r}$ ... Then $$\mathop{\mathrm{cat}}M = r + 1.$$* :::
nodes.statement: Theorem 1.15 (1.13). Let $M = S^{k_1} \times S^{k_2} \times \ldots \times S^{k_r}$ be a product of $k_i$-dimensional spheres, $i = 1, \ldots, r$. Then the Lyusternik--Shnirelman category of $M$ is one more than the number $r$ of factors: $\mathop{\mathrm{cat}}M = r + 1$.

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#thm:1.14 .theorem} **Theorem 1.16** (1.14). *Let $M = S^{k_1} \times \ldots \times S^{k_r}$ and $P = S^{k_{i_1}} \times \ldots \times S^{k_{i_l}}$ a submanifold. Then $$\mathop{\mathrm{P\text{-}cat}}M = r - l + 1.$$* :::
nodes.statement: Theorem 1.16 (1.14). Let $M = S^{k_1} \times S^{k_2} \times \ldots \times S^{k_r}$ be a product of $k_i$-dimensional spheres, $k_i \geq 1$, $i = 1, \ldots, r$, and let $P = S^{k_{i_1}} \times S^{k_{i_2}} \times \ldots \times S^{k_{i_l}}$ be a submanifold of $M$, where $\{k_{i_1}, k_{i_2}, \ldots, k_{i_l}\} \subset \{k_1, k_2, \ldots, k_r\}$. Then the $P$-category of $M$ equals $\mathop{\mathrm{P\text{-}cat}}M = r - l + 1$.

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#cor:1.15 .corollary} **Corollary 1.17** (1.15). *Let $P$ be the $k$-dim torus. Then $$T^k\text{-}\mathop{\mathrm{cat}}T^n = n - k + 1,\quad n \geq k.$$* :::
nodes.statement: Corollary 1.17 (1.15). Let $P$ be the $k$-dimensional torus. Then the $P$-category of the $n$-dimensional torus equals $T^k\text{-}\mathop{\mathrm{cat}}T^n = n - k + 1$, $n \geq k$.

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#prop:1.16 .proposition} **Proposition 1.18** (1.16). *Let $P$ be the $l$-dim sphere. Then $S^l$-cat $S^n$ equals: 1. two if $l < n$; 2. one if $l = n$; 3. zero if $l > n$.* :::
nodes.statement: Proposition 1.18 (1.16). Let $P$ be the $l$-dimensional sphere. Then the $P$-category of the $n$-dimensional sphere equals: 1. two, if $l < n$; 2. one, if $l = n$; 3. zero, if $l > n$.

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#def:2.1 .definition} **Definition 2.1** (2.1). A differentiable function on a manifold whose set of critical points is a disjoint union of smooth submanifolds without boundary is called a *$P$-function* if each critical submanifold is homeomorphic to a fixed smooth manifold $P$ without boundary. :::
nodes.statement: Definition 2.1 (2.1). A differentiable function on a manifold whose set of critical points is a disjoint union of smooth submanifolds without boundary is called a $P$-function if each of its critical submanifolds is homeomorphic to a fixed smooth manifold $P$ without boundary.

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#prop:2.2 .proposition} **Proposition 2.2** (2.2). *Let $P$ be a smooth submanifold of dimension $p$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, and let $f\colon P \times \mathbb{R}^{n-p} \to \mathbb{R}$ ... Then there exists $F\colon P \times \mathbb{R}^{n-p} \to \mathbb{R}$ with a unique critical submanifold $P$ and $F=f$ outside a compact set $C$.* :::
nodes.statement: Proposition 2.2 (2.2). Let $P$ be a smooth submanifold of dimension $p$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, and let $f\colon P \times \mathbb{R}^{n-p} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function with the properties: $f$ is continuous; the submanifold $P$ lies in a level surface; $f|_{P \times \mathbb{R}^{n-p}\setminus C}$ is differentiable and has no critical points. Then on $P \times \mathbb{R}^{n-p}$ there exists a function $F\colon P \times \mathbb{R}^{n-p} \to \mathbb{R}$, having the properties: $F$ has a unique critical submanifold $P$; $F|_{P \times \mathbb{R}^{n-p}\setminus C} = f|_{P \times \mathbb{R}^{n-p}\setminus C}$ for some compact set $C \subset P \times \mathbb{R}^{n-p}$.

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#def:2.3 .definition} **Definition 2.3** (2.3). [@takens-1968] Let $Q^m$ be a manifold with boundary ... A homeomorphism $\varphi\colon Q^m \to \widetilde{Q}^m$ ... is called a *special almost diffeomorphism*. A composition of a diffeomorphism and a special almost diffeomorphism is called an *almost diffeomorphism*. :::
nodes.statement: Definition 2.3 (2.3). [Takens] Let $Q^m$ be a manifold with boundary, and let $S$ be the set of points at which $\partial Q^m$ fails to be smooth. Assume that every point of $S$ has a neighbourhood in $Q^m$ diffeomorphic to $\{(x_1,\ldots,x_m) \in \mathbb{R}^m : x_1 \geq 0, x_2 \geq 0\}$. $Q^m$ admits a unique smoothing $\widetilde{Q}^m$. A homeomorphism $\varphi\colon Q^m \to \widetilde{Q}^m$ that is a diffeomorphism $Q^m \setminus S \to \widetilde{Q}^m \setminus \varphi(S)$, as well as its inverse, is called a special almost diffeomorphism. A map obtained as a composition of a diffeomorphism and a special almost diffeomorphism is called an almost diffeomorphism.

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#prop:2.4 .proposition} **Proposition 2.4** (2.4). *Let $M^m$ be a smooth compact manifold with boundary $= M_1 \sqcup M_2$ admitting a covering $\{Q_i\}_{i=1}^{3}$ ... Then there exists a $P$-function $F\colon M^m \to \mathbb{R}$ constant min on $M_1$, constant max on $M_2$, no critical points on $M_1,M_2$, with unique critical submanifold $P$ in $\mathop{\mathrm{Int}}M^m$.* :::
nodes.statement: Proposition 2.4 (2.4). Let $M^m$ be a smooth compact manifold with boundary $\partial M^m$, which is a disjoint union of closed subsets $M_1$ and $M_2$, and let $(M^m; M_1, M_2)$ admit a covering $\{Q_i\}_{i=1}^{3}$ by three closed submanifolds satisfying: $\mathop{\mathrm{Int}}(Q_i) \cap \mathop{\mathrm{Int}}(Q_j) = \emptyset$, $i \neq j$; $(Q_i, M_i)$ is almost diffeomorphic to $(M_i \times [0,1], M_i \times \{0\})$ for $i = 1, 2$; $Q_3$ is almost diffeomorphic to $P \times D^{m-p}$, where $P$ is a smooth submanifold of $M^m$ of dimension $p$; $Q_1 \cap Q_2$ is a smooth submanifold of $M^m \setminus \mathop{\mathrm{Int}}Q_3$. Then on $M^m$ there exists a $P$-function $F\colon M^m \to \mathbb{R}$ with the following properties: $F$ takes a constant minimal value on $M_1$; $F$ takes a constant maximal value on $M_2$; $F$ has no critical points on $M_1$ or $M_2$; $F$ has a unique critical submanifold $P$ lying in $\mathop{\mathrm{Int}}M^m$.

nodes.source_tex: ::: remark **Remark 2.5**. If $M_1 = \emptyset$ or $M_2 = \emptyset$, then $Q_1$ or $Q_2$, respectively, is omitted from the covering $\{Q_i\}_{i=1}^{3}$. :::
nodes.statement: Remark 2.5. If $M_1 = \emptyset$ or $M_2 = \emptyset$, then $Q_1$ or $Q_2$, respectively, is omitted from the covering $\{Q_i\}_{i=1}^{3}$.

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#thm:2.5 .theorem} **Theorem 2.6** (2.5). *Let $M^m$ be a smooth compact manifold and $M_1 \subset \ldots \subset M_k = M^m$ a filtration satisfying conditions 1-4 (each layer covered as in Proposition 2.4). Then on $M^m$ there exists a $P$-function with $k$ critical submanifolds.* :::
nodes.statement: Theorem 2.6 (2.5). Let $M^m$ be a smooth compact manifold (with or without boundary), and let $M_1 \subset M_2 \subset \ldots \subset M_k = M^m$ be a filtration of $M^m$ by compact manifolds with boundary, satisfying: 1. $M_i$ are manifolds with boundary, $i = 1, \ldots, k-1$; 2. $M_i \subset \mathop{\mathrm{Int}}(M_{i+1})$, $i = 1, \ldots, k-1$; 3. $\partial M^m \subset M_k \setminus M_{k-1}$; 4. for each $i = 1, \ldots, k$, the manifold $(M_i \setminus \mathop{\mathrm{Int}}M_{i-1}; \partial M_{i-1}, \partial M_i)$ admits a covering by three closed subsets as in Proposition 2.4. Then on $M^m$ there exists a $P$-function with $k$ critical submanifolds.

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#def:2.6 .definition} **Definition 2.7** (2.6). Let $P$ be a critical submanifold of $f$ on $M$, $f(P)=0$. An *integral trajectory* $L$ of $\mathrm{grad}\, f$ *enters* $P$ if it is defined for small $f$ and every decreasing sequence converges to $a \in P$. $L$ *leaves* $a \in P$ if for $-f$ it enters $a$. :::
nodes.statement: Definition 2.7 (2.6). Let $P$ be a critical submanifold of a function $f$ on a manifold $M$, and $f(P) = 0$. We say that an integral trajectory $L$ of the vector field $\mathrm{grad}\, f$ enters $P$ if it is defined for all sufficiently small values of $f$; every sequence of points $a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots$ of $L$ for which $f(a_1), f(a_2), f(a_3), \ldots$ decreases to $p$, converges to a point $a \in P$. An integral trajectory $L$ leaves a point $a \in P$ if for the function $-f$ it enters the point $a$.

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#prop:2.7 .proposition} **Proposition 2.8** (2.7). *An integral trajectory of $\mathrm{grad}\, f$ through an arbitrary point of $U$ either enters $P$, or leaves $P$, or reaches the boundary $\partial \overline{U}$.* :::
nodes.statement: Proposition 2.8 (2.7). An integral trajectory of $\mathrm{grad}\, f$ passing through an arbitrary point of $U$ either enters $P$, or leaves $P$, or reaches the boundary $\partial \overline{U}$ at some point.

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#def:2.8 .definition} **Definition 2.9** (2.8). Let $V$ be a neighbourhood of $P$ with $v = V \cap f^{-1}(p) \subset U$. A subset $C_\varepsilon(P)$ of $U$ is a *cylindrical neighbourhood* of $P$ if for small $\varepsilon>0$ it contains the listed trajectory points and the submanifold $P$. :::
nodes.statement: Definition 2.9 (2.8). Let $V$ be a neighbourhood of a critical submanifold $P$ in $M$ such that $v = V \cap f^{-1}(p) \subset U$. A subset $C_\varepsilon(P)$ of $U$ is called a cylindrical neighbourhood of $P$ in $M$ if, for sufficiently small $\varepsilon > 0$, it contains: the points $x$ of all integral trajectories of $\mathrm{grad}\, f$ entering $P$ for which $p < f(x) < p + \varepsilon$; the points $x$ of all integral trajectories of $\mathrm{grad}\, f$ leaving $P$ for which $p - \varepsilon < f(x) < p$; the points $x$ of all integral trajectories of $\mathrm{grad}\, f$ passing through points of $v$ distinct from $P$ for which $p - \varepsilon < f(x) < p + \varepsilon$; the submanifold $P$.

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#prop:2.9 .proposition} **Proposition 2.10** (2.9). *There exists $\varepsilon > 0$ small enough that the points described in items a)--d) of Definition 2.9 lie in $U$.* :::
nodes.statement: Proposition 2.10 (2.9). There exists $\varepsilon > 0$ small enough that the points described in items a)--d) of Definition 2.9 lie in $U$.

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#cor:2.10 .corollary} **Corollary 2.11** (2.10). *The tubular neighbourhood of a critical submanifold $P$ in $M$ contains arbitrarily small cylindrical neighbourhoods of $P$.* :::
nodes.statement: Corollary 2.11 (2.10). The tubular neighbourhood of a critical submanifold $P$ in $M$ contains arbitrarily small cylindrical neighbourhoods of $P$.

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#prop:2.11 .proposition} **Proposition 2.12** (2.11). *The set $C_\varepsilon(P)$ is a neighbourhood of $P$ in $M$, i.e. a subset of $M$ containing arbitrarily small tubular neighbourhoods of $P$.* :::
nodes.statement: Proposition 2.12 (2.11). The set $C_\varepsilon(P)$ is a neighbourhood of $P$ in $M$, that is, a subset of $M$ containing arbitrarily small tubular neighbourhoods of $P$ in $M$.

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#thm:2.12 .theorem} **Theorem 2.13** (2.12). *Let $M$ be a smooth compact connected manifold and $f$ a $P$-function (constant max, no critical points on boundary if any). Then the number of critical submanifolds of $f$ is at least the $P$-category of $M$.* :::
nodes.statement: Theorem 2.13 (2.12). Let $M$ be a smooth compact connected manifold (with or without boundary), and let $f$ be a $P$-function on it which, in the case of a manifold with boundary, takes a constant maximal value on the boundary and has no critical points on the boundary. Then the number of critical submanifolds of $f$ is at least the $P$-category of $M$.

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#def:2.13 .definition} **Definition 2.14** (2.13). A $P$-function is called *exact* if the number of its critical submanifolds equals the minimum over all $P$-functions of that number. :::
nodes.statement: Definition 2.14 (2.13). A $P$-function is called exact on a manifold if the number of its critical submanifolds equals the minimum, taken over all $P$-functions on the manifold, of the number of critical submanifolds.

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#def:2.14 .definition} **Definition 2.15** (2.14). A $P$-function is called *round* if its critical submanifolds are homeomorphic to the circle $S^1$. :::
nodes.statement: Definition 2.15 (2.14). A $P$-function on a manifold is called round if its critical submanifolds are homeomorphic to the circle $S^1$.

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#thm:2.15 .theorem} **Theorem 2.16** (2.15). *Let $P = S^{k_{i_1}} \times \ldots \times S^{k_{i_l}}$ ... Then on $M = S^{k_1} \times \ldots \times S^{k_n}$ there exists an exact $P$-function with $n - l + 1$ singularities.* :::
nodes.statement: Theorem 2.16 (2.15). Let $\{k_{i_1}, \ldots, k_{i_l}\}$ be a subset of $\{k_1, \ldots, k_n\}$ positive integers. Let $P = S^{k_{i_1}} \times \ldots \times S^{k_{i_l}}$ be a product of $k_{i_j}$-dimensional spheres, $j = 1, \ldots, l$. Then on the manifold $M = S^{k_1} \times \ldots \times S^{k_n}$ there exists an exact $P$-function with $n - l + 1$ singularities.

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#cor:2.16 .corollary} **Corollary 2.17** (2.16). *Let $P$ be the $k$-dim torus, $k \leq n$. Then on $T^n$ there exists an exact $P$-function with $n - k + 1$ singularities; in particular an exact round function on $T^n$ has $n$ singularities.* :::
nodes.statement: Corollary 2.17 (2.16). Let $P$ be the $k$-dimensional torus, $k \leq n$. Then on the $n$-dimensional torus there exists an exact $P$-function with $n - k + 1$ singularities. In particular, an exact round function on the $n$-dimensional torus has $n$ singularities.

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#thm:2.17 .theorem} **Theorem 2.18** (2.17). *Let $P = S^n$. Then on $S^{2n+1}$, $n \geq 1$, there exists an exact $P$-function with two singularities.* :::
nodes.statement: Theorem 2.18 (2.17). Let $P = S^n$ be the $n$-dimensional sphere. Then on the odd-dimensional sphere $S^{2n+1}$, $n \geq 1$, there exists an exact $P$-function with two singularities.

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#prop:3.1 .proposition} **Proposition 3.1** (3.1). *On a 2-dim smooth compact connected manifold with boundary, not homeomorphic to $D^2$, there exists an exact function with two critical points.* :::
nodes.statement: Proposition 3.1 (3.1). On a two-dimensional smooth compact connected manifold with boundary, not homeomorphic to the disc $D^2$, there exists an exact function with two critical points.

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#thm:3.2 .theorem} **Theorem 3.2** (3.2). *On a manifold homeomorphic to $S^2$, $\mathbb{R}P^2$, or $D^2$ there exist no round functions. On every other 2-dim smooth compact connected manifold round functions exist.* :::
nodes.statement: Theorem 3.2 (3.2). On a manifold homeomorphic to the sphere $S^2$, to the projective plane $\mathbb{R}P^2$, or to the disc $D^2$, there exist no round functions. On every other two-dimensional smooth compact connected manifold round functions exist.

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#thm:3.3 .theorem} **Theorem 3.3** (3.3). *On every 2-dim smooth compact connected manifold not homeomorphic to $D^2$, $S^2$, $\mathbb{R}P^2$, there exists an exact round function with: 1. two singularities on torus and Klein bottle; 2. three on remaining without boundary; 3. one on $S^1 \times I$ and Möbius band; 4. two on remaining with boundary.* :::
nodes.statement: Theorem 3.3 (3.3). On every two-dimensional smooth compact connected manifold not homeomorphic to the disc $D^2$, the sphere $S^2$ or the projective plane $\mathbb{R}P^2$, there exists an exact round function whose number of singularities equals: 1. two on the torus and the Klein bottle; 2. three on the remaining manifolds without boundary; 3. one on the annulus $S^1 \times I$ and on the Möbius band; 4. two on the remaining manifolds with boundary.

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#thm:3.4 .theorem} **Theorem 3.4** (3.4). *On every 3-dim smooth compact connected manifold without boundary a round function exists. If ~= $S^3$, $\mathbb{R}P^3$, $S^1 \times S^2$, or a lens space: exact round function with two critical circles. If ~= $T^3$: exact round function with three critical circles. Otherwise: a round function with at most four singularities.* :::
nodes.statement: Theorem 3.4 (3.4). On every three-dimensional smooth compact connected manifold without boundary a round function exists. If the manifold is homeomorphic to one of the sphere $S^3$, the projective space $\mathbb{R}P^3$, the manifold $S^1 \times S^2$, a lens space, then it admits an exact round function with two critical circles. If the manifold is homeomorphic to the torus $T^3$, then it admits an exact round function with three critical circles. On every other three-dimensional smooth compact connected manifold there exists a round function whose number of singularities does not exceed four.

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#thm:3.5 .theorem} **Theorem 3.5** (3.5). *Let $P = S^{n-1}$. Then on the $n$-dimensional sphere there are no $P$-functions.* :::
nodes.statement: Theorem 3.5 (3.5). Let $P = S^{n-1}$ be the $(n-1)$-dimensional sphere. Then on the $n$-dimensional sphere there are no $P$-functions.

nodes.source_tex: ::: {#thm:3.6 .theorem} **Theorem 3.6** (3.6). *Let $P = S^1$ and $n \geq 3$. Then on the $n$-dimensional sphere there exists a $P$-function whose number of singularities does not exceed $$[n/2] + 1.$$* :::
nodes.statement: Theorem 3.6 (3.6). Let $P = S^1$ be the one-dimensional sphere, and let $n \geq 3$. Then on the $n$-dimensional sphere there exists a $P$-function whose number of singularities does not exceed $[n/2] + 1$.

Proof of Theorem 1.7 (1.5). Consider cycles $c_1, \ldots, c_q$ in $H_*(M)$ of dimension less than $m$ whose intersection is a cycle not homologous to zero of dimension at least $p$, and $q = \mathrm{long}^{p} M$. Suppose $\mathop{\mathrm{P\text{-}cat}}M = s \leq q$. Then there exist closed subsets $A_1, \ldots, A_s$ in $M$ contracting to $P$ whose union is $M$; WLOG $s = q$ and $M = \bigcup_{i=1}^{q} A_i$. If $q = 1$, conditions 1') and 3') of Definition 1.5 imply $p < m$, and P-cat cannot be one, so it is at least two. For $q \geq 2$, condition 3') gives $\dim c_i > p$. Since each $A_i$ contracts to $P$, the exact homology sequence of the pair gives $i_* = 0$ for $l > p$, so $H_l(M) = H_l(M, A_i)$ and each $c_i$ is homologous to $\gamma_i$ supported in $M \setminus A_i$. Intersecting, $0 \neq c = c_1 \cap \ldots \cap c_q \sim \gamma_1 \cap \ldots \cap \gamma_q = \gamma \subset M \setminus \bigcup A_i = \emptyset$, a contradiction. For a manifold with boundary, suppose P-cat $M = s \leq q - 1$; analogously $\gamma = \bigcap_{i=1}^{q-1}\gamma_i$ lies in $\partial M$ and, with $c_q$ in general position, $0 \neq c \sim \gamma \cap c_q = \emptyset$. This contradiction completes the proof.

Proof of Proposition 1.8 (1.6). All cycles are realised as simplicial subcomplexes in general position. If $p = 0$, the cycles must be zero- or one-dimensional (Property (1)'); if a zero-dimensional cycle appears, $q = 1$ by Remark 1.6, so $\mathrm{long}^{p} M \geq 1$. For $M \cong (N;\partial N)$ or $(L;\partial L)$, one-dimensional cycles in general position do not intersect, so $q = 1$; on other manifolds with boundary the maximal number is two. If $M \cong S^2$ then $H_1(M) = 0$, so $c$ in Definition 1.5 is zero-dimensional and $q = 1$. For $M$ without boundary not $\cong S^2$, by the classification of surfaces it is a sphere with handles or Möbius bands, and the maximal number of one-dimensional cycles with intersection not homologous to zero is two. If $p = 1$, the cycles are one-dimensional and their number is at most one; the $p$-length is one if a one-dimensional cycle not homologous to zero exists and zero otherwise. Since $H^1(S^2) = 0$ and $H_1(M) \neq 0$ for other surfaces without boundary, the statement follows.

Proof of Theorem 1.9 (1.7). All cycles are in general position and realised as simplicial complexes. From $\{k_1, \ldots, k_r\}$ choose $l$ elements $k_{i_1}, \ldots, k_{i_l}$ whose sum is at least $p$. The submanifold $Q = S^{k_{i_1}} \times \ldots \times S^{k_{i_l}}$ is a cycle of dimension $\sum k_{i_j}$. Multiplying $Q$ by each remaining factor yields $r - l$ cycles $c_1, \ldots, c_{r-l}$ with $\dim c_i < n$ (if $l+1 \leq r$), $\dim \bigcap c_i \geq p$ since $\bigcap c_i = Q$, and $Q$ not homologous to zero. Thus they satisfy conditions 1)'-3)' of $p$-length, so taking the minimal $l$ gives $\mathrm{long}^{p} M \geq r - \min l(p)$. Then Theorem 1.7 (thm:1.5) together with the estimate from Theorem 1.16 (thm:1.14), $\mathop{\mathrm{P\text{-}cat}}M \leq r - l + 1$, yields the statement.

Proof of Corollary 1.10 (1.8). Since $p = 0$, take as cycles forming the length of $M$ the spheres $S^{k_j}$, $j = 1, \ldots, r$. Their intersection is a single point, a cycle of dimension 0 not homologous to zero.
The following proposition (Proposition 1.11 / 1.9) is an immediate consequence of Theorem 1.9 (thm:1.7).

Proof of Proposition 1.12 (1.10). Since any two-dimensional compact connected manifold $M$ with boundary is homeomorphic to a sphere with holes and handles or Möbius bands, $M$ is covered by two discs: an orientable manifold with a single hole as in Fig. 1.3(a); if there are several boundary components, the first categorical set is combined with the set that cuts the holes so that the union is a disc and the remainder is a disc. In the non-orientable case, a manifold with one boundary component is covered by two subsets as in Fig. 1.4 (a sphere with three Möbius bands and one hole); the first categorical set takes parts of the Möbius bands glued into the holes combined with the shaded portion; for more boundary components the cutting set is added. Removing this disc-subset leaves a closure also homeomorphic to $D^2$.

Proof of Proposition 1.13 (1.11). In the first case the statement is clear. In the second case, a manifold with boundary not $\cong S^1 \times I$ or Möbius band cannot have round category one (its homologies prevent it), so it is at least two; representing it as a sphere with holes and handles, with one boundary component it is covered by two closed subsets each contracting to a circle (Fig. 1.5), and for several components the cutting set is adjoined; non-orientable manifolds are handled via Möbius bands (Fig. 1.6). In the third case ($S^2$, $\mathbb{R}P^2$, $T^2$, Klein bottle) each is covered by two annuli $S^1 \times I$. For any other manifold without boundary the round category cannot be one or two (a counting argument on circles non-homologous to zero, using rank of $H_1 \geq 4$, gives a contradiction), so it is at least three; representing the orientable manifold as a sphere with handles (Fig. 1.7) and the non-orientable via Fig. 1.4, three closed subsets each contracting to a circle suffice. Hence it equals three.

Proof of Proposition 1.14 (1.12). In the first case each listed manifold has Heegaard genus one and is the gluing of two solid tori $S^1 \times D^2$ along a boundary homeomorphism, so the statement is clear. If $M \cong T^3$, then by Proposition 1.11 (prop:1.9) its $p$-length equals two (with $p=1$), and by Theorem 1.7 (thm:1.5) the round category is at least three; writing $T^3 = S^1 \times T^2$ and using $\mathrm{cat}\,T^2 = 3$, $T^3 = \bigcup_{i=1}^3 S^1 \times A_i$ each contracting to $S^1$, so the round category is exactly three. All other 3-manifolds without boundary have Heegaard genus greater than one, are gluings of two handlebodies, and each handlebody is a union of two closed subsets each contracting to a circle (Fig. 1.8).

Proof of Theorem 1.15 (1.13). By Corollary 1.10 (cor:1.8) $\mathrm{long}\, M = r$, so by Theorem 1.7 (thm:1.5) $\mathop{\mathrm{cat}}M \geq r + 1$. Realise $M$ as the joint level set of the standard sphere equations in $\mathbb{R}^l$, $l = \sum k_i + r$, and define $f = x_1 + y_1 + \ldots + z_1$. Its restriction to $M$ has one maximum $r$, one minimum $-r$, and critical points on $r - 1$ connected level surfaces $\{f = -r+2\}, \ldots, \{f = r-2\}$; merging the critical points on each level surface into one degenerate critical point [Milnor] gives $r + 1$ critical points, so $M$ is covered by $r+1$ contractible closed subsets. Hence $\mathop{\mathrm{cat}}M = r + 1$.

Proof of Theorem 1.16 (1.14). By Theorem 1.9 (thm:1.7) $\mathrm{long}^{p} M \geq r - l$. By Theorem 1.7 (thm:1.5) $\mathop{\mathrm{P\text{-}cat}}M \geq r - l + 1$. For the reverse, write $M = P \times L$ where $L$ is the product of the remaining $r - l$ spheres; by Theorem 1.15 (thm:1.13) $\mathop{\mathrm{cat}}L = r - l + 1$, so $L = \bigcup_{i=1}^{r-l+1} A_i$ with each $A_i$ contracting in $L$ to a point. Then $M = \bigcup_{i=1}^{r-l+1} P \times A_i$ with each $P \times A_i$ contracting in $M$ to $P$, giving $\mathop{\mathrm{P\text{-}cat}}M \leq r - l + 1$. Combined with the opposite inequality, $\mathop{\mathrm{P\text{-}cat}}M = r - l + 1$.

Proof of Proposition 1.18 (1.16). If $l \neq n$, then $S^l\text{-}\mathop{\mathrm{cat}}S^n \neq 1$ (the homologies of spheres prevent it). If $l < n$, cover $S^n$ by two closed discs $D_1, D_2$ meeting along the equator; since $n > l$, into each disc inscribe an $S^l$-sphere meeting the equator in one point ($S_1^l \subset D_2^n$, $S_2^l \subset D_1^n$), and take $S_1^l \cup D_1^n$ and $S_2^l \cup D_2^n$ as categorical subsets, giving category two. The cases $l = n$ and $l > n$ give one and zero respectively.

Proof of Proposition 2.2 (2.2). Let $f(P) = 0$ and $U = P \times U'$ a bounded neighbourhood. Consider a tubular neighbourhood $T_r(P)$ and $v = T_r(P) \cap f^{-1}(0)$; choose $\varepsilon > 0$ so the cylindrical neighbourhood $C_\varepsilon(P)$ is bounded. Use the retraction $\pi\colon C_\varepsilon(P) \to v$ along trajectories of $\mathrm{grad}\, f$. Modify $f$ only on $C = C_\varepsilon(P)$ using auxiliary functions $\lambda\colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ and $H\colon v \to [0,1]$ with the stated properties, and set $F(x) = f(x)$ off $C_\varepsilon(P)$ and $F(x) = (1 - H\pi(x))\lambda(f(x)) + H\pi(x) f(x)$ on $C_\varepsilon(P)$. Properties (1),(1') make $F$ differentiable, (2),(2') make it agree with $f$ near the boundary, so $F$ is differentiable on its domain and (b) holds with $C = \overline{C_\varepsilon(P)}$. Computing $\langle dF, \mathrm{grad}\, f\rangle$ shows the derivative is positive everywhere on $C_\varepsilon(P)$ except on $P$, so $F$ has $P$ as unique critical submanifold. The functions $\lambda$ (as in Takens, via a series $\lambda = \sum a_i \lambda_i$) and $H$ (via nested tubular neighbourhoods and bump functions $\varphi_{r_0 - r_i}$, $H = \sum b_i h_i|_{N_i}$) are constructed with the required properties, completing the proof.

Proof of Proposition 2.4 (2.4). Since $(Q_i, M_i)$ is almost diffeomorphic to $(M_i \times [0,1], M_i \times \{0\})$, there are homeomorphisms $\varphi_i\colon Q_i \to M_i \times [0,1]$; with $\phi_i(x,t) = 1 - t$ form $f_i = \phi_i \circ \varphi_i$ and define $f$ on $Q_1 \cup Q_2$ by $-f_1$ on $Q_1$ and $f_2$ on $Q_2$, differentiable with no critical points off $Q_1 \cap Q_2$. Modify $f$ near $Q_1 \cap Q_2$ using a tubular neighbourhood diffeomorphism and a function $\theta = \theta'' \circ (\theta')^{-1}$ so it becomes differentiable on $Q_1 \cup Q_2 \setminus (Q_1 \cap Q_2 \cap Q_3)$ without critical points. Using charts $\varphi_p$ adapted to $Q_1, Q_2, Q_3$ near $Q_1 \cap Q_2 \cap Q_3$, define $\bar f$ equal to $\theta$ on $T'(Q_1 \cap Q_2)$ and $f$ off a neighbourhood, extended by zero on $Q_3$; then $\bar f$ is continuous, differentiable with no critical points off $Q_3$, with $\bar f(M_1) = -1$, $\bar f(M_2) = 1$, $\bar f(Q_3) = 0$. Since $Q_3$ is almost diffeomorphic to $P \times D^{m-p}$, a map $\Phi$ collapses $Q_3$ to $P$; the composition $\bar f \circ \Phi^{-1}$ is continuous, differentiable off $P$, with no critical points outside $P$. Applying Proposition 2.2 (prop:2.2) near $P$ yields the required function.

Proof of Theorem 2.6 (2.5). On each layer $(M_i \setminus \mathop{\mathrm{Int}}M_{i-1}; \partial M_{i-1}, \partial M_i)$ construct $F_i$ as in Proposition 2.4 (prop:2.4) with $F_i(\partial M_{i-1}) = i-1$, $F_i(\partial M_i) = i$, no critical points on the boundaries, and a single critical submanifold inside. The function $F(x) = F_i(x)$ on each layer is continuous with one critical submanifold per layer. To make it differentiable, equip $M^m$ with a metric $\rho$ and correct the $F_i$ near the boundaries via functions $f_i$ equal to $i - \rho(x, \partial M_i)$, $i - 1 + \rho(x, \partial M_{i-1})$, or $F_i(x)$ on the respective regions. The resulting $\bar F$ is a $P$-function with $k$ critical submanifolds.

Proof of Proposition 2.8 (2.7). Let $L$ be a segment of an integral trajectory through a point of $U$, traversed in the direction of decreasing $f$, contained in $U$. Since $f$ is bounded on $U$, let $\beta = \inf_L f$ and pick a sequence $a_1, a_2, \ldots$ on $L$ with $f(a_i) \downarrow \beta$. The sequence converges (otherwise two limit points contradict the ball-neighbourhood argument). It cannot converge to a point of $U$ off $P$, since $U$ open would contain trajectory points with $f$ below $\beta$. Hence the limit is a point of $P$ or of the boundary of $\overline{U}$; an analogous statement holds for the opposite direction.

Proof of Proposition 2.10 (2.9). Let $W_\eta = \{x : \rho(x, v) < \eta\}$ with $\overline{W_\eta} \subset U$. Suppose for contradiction that for every $\varepsilon$ there are points of type a)-d) of Definition 2.9 outside $W_\eta$; by Proposition 2.8 (prop:2.7) they lie on $\partial \overline{W_\eta}$. For $\varepsilon = 1/i$ choose $q_i \to q \in \partial \overline{W_\eta}$, a non-critical point; since $|f(q_i)| \leq p + 1/i$, $f(q) = p$. A cylindrical neighbourhood of $q$ disjoint from $v$ contains almost all $q_i$ and the intersection points of their trajectories with $f^{-1}(p)$, which then cannot lie in $v$, a contradiction.
Proof of Corollary 2.11 (2.10). The proof follows from the fact that in $M$ one can find a tubular neighbourhood of $P$ contained in $U$ and containing the closure of $W_\eta$.

Proof of Proposition 2.12 (2.11). Choose a small tubular neighbourhood $T$ of $P$ with $|f| < p + \varepsilon$ on $T$ and $T \cap f^{-1}(p) \subset C_\varepsilon(P)$. If $C_\varepsilon(P)$ were not a neighbourhood of $P$, there would be $a_i \to a \in P$ in $T$ outside $C_\varepsilon(P)$; WLOG $f(a_i) > p$. The trajectory through each $a_i$ in the decreasing direction cannot enter $P$ or pass through $v$, so by Proposition 2.8 (prop:2.7) it reaches $\partial \overline{T}$ at $b_i$ with $f(b_i) \geq p$ and $f(b_i) \to p$. A limit point $b$ on $\partial \overline{T}$ has $f(b) = p$, but every cylindrical neighbourhood of $b$ contains infinitely many $a_i$ and $b_i$, contradicting $a_i \to a \in P$.

Proof of Theorem 2.13 (2.12). By compactness $f$ has finitely many critical submanifolds and values; argue by induction on the number of critical values. For the minimal value $a$ with critical submanifolds $P_1, \ldots, P_k$, $M^{a+\varepsilon}$ is a disjoint union of closures of cylindrical neighbourhoods, and since each has P-category one, $\mathop{\mathrm{P\text{-}cat}}M^{a+\varepsilon} = k$. Assume for value $b$ that $k \geq \mathop{\mathrm{P\text{-}cat}}M^{b+\varepsilon}$. For the next value $c$ with critical submanifolds $P_1, \ldots, P_s$, choose disjoint tubular neighbourhoods within the critical layer; then $M^{b+\varepsilon}$ is a deformation retract of the closure of $M^{c+\delta}$ minus the cylindrical neighbourhoods $\overline{C_\delta(P_i)}$, each of which has P-category one. By the subadditivity of P-category, $\mathop{\mathrm{P\text{-}cat}}M^{c+\delta} \leq \mathop{\mathrm{P\text{-}cat}}M^{b+\varepsilon} + s \leq k + s$, completing the induction.

Proof of Theorem 2.16 (2.15). By Theorem 1.16 (thm:1.14) the number of singularities of a $P$-function on $M$ is at least $n - l + 1$. Write $M = P \times L$ with $P = S^{k_1} \times \ldots \times S^{k_l}$ and $L = S^{k_{l+1}} \times \ldots \times S^{k_n}$ realised in $\mathbb{R}^m$. Define $f(P, x_1, \ldots, y_{k_n+1}) = x_1 + \ldots + y_1$ on $P \times \mathbb{R}^m$; its restriction to $L$ has one minimum, one maximum, and critical points on $n - l - 1$ connected level surfaces, which can be merged into single degenerate critical points [Milnor, p. 206], giving $n - l + 1$ critical points. Its restriction to $M$ is the desired exact $P$-function.

Proof of Theorem 2.18 (2.17). Realize $S^{2n+1} = D^{2n+1}/S^{2n}$ and write the disc as the union of three subsets $N_1, N_2, N_3$ (defined by inequalities on the $x_i^2$) for small $\varepsilon > 0$. After the quotient, cover $S^{2n+1}$ by $M_1$ and $M_2$, the images of $N_1 \cup N_2$ and $N_3$; each is almost diffeomorphic to $S^n \times D^{n+1}$. Hence the statement follows from Theorem 2.6 (thm:2.5).

Proof of Proposition 3.1 (3.1). Any two-dimensional compact connected manifold with boundary admits a filtration $M_1 \subset M_2 = M$ satisfying the hypotheses of Theorem 2.6 (thm:2.5), following from the covering of the manifold by two discs (Fig. 1.3). By Proposition 1.12 (prop:1.10) and Theorem 2.13 (thm:2.12), the constructed function is exact.

Proof of Theorem 3.2 (3.2). Suppose a round function $f$ exists on $S^2$; it has finitely many critical circles. For a critical value $c$, remove the critical layer $f^{-1}[c - \varepsilon, c + \varepsilon]$; by Jordan's theorem the remainder is a disjoint union $D_1 \cup D_2$ each with one boundary component, and each must contain critical circles (else it would be $\partial D_i \times I$ with two boundary components). Iterating the removal of critical layers exhausts the critical values but leaves a submanifold with a single boundary component that must still contain critical points, a contradiction. Analogous arguments rule out round functions on $\mathbb{R}P^2$ and $D^2$. On every other two-dimensional manifold without boundary (other than $S^2$, $\mathbb{R}P^2$) round functions exist, e.g. the height function (Fig. 3.2) or via level lines on the fundamental polygon; on manifolds with boundary they are obtained by gluing a copy $N$ and cutting along level lines.

Proof of Theorem 3.3 (3.3). For the torus $T^2 = S^1 \times S^1$ the restriction of $f = x_1$ is an exact function with two critical circles; the Klein bottle, obtained from the torus by cutting and identifying, similarly admits $f = x_1$ exact with two critical circles. On remaining manifolds without boundary an exact function is defined by smooth level lines: since such a manifold is covered by three closed sets $Q_1, Q_2, Q_3$ each $\cong S^1 \times I$ (Proposition 1.13 / prop:1.11), take circles $S^1 \times t_0$ as level surfaces and extend across the intersection arcs. On the annulus $S^1 \times I$ the function $f = (x_3 - 0.5)^2$ has one critical circle and is exact; the Möbius band similarly. On the remaining manifolds with boundary a round function is defined via level lines analogously.

Proof of Theorem 3.4 (3.4). If a 3-manifold is $\cong S^3$, $\mathbb{R}P^3$, $S^1 \times S^2$, or a lens space, it has a Heegaard diagram of genus one and is the gluing of two solid tori $S^1 \times D^2$; defining on one solid torus a differentiable function with constant maximal value on the boundary and one critical circle, and extending to the other by the negative plus a constant, gives an exact round function (exactness follows from the main theorem and Proposition 1.14 / prop:1.12). If $\cong T^3$, by Corollary 2.17 (cor:2.16) there is an exact round function with three critical circles. Any other such manifold $M$ has Heegaard genus $g \geq 2$ and is the gluing of two handlebodies; cutting each into parts $N_i \cong S^1 \times D^2$ and defining on $M_1$ a function with constant maximal value $a$ on $\partial M_1$ and two critical circles (as in Theorem 2.6 / thm:2.5), the function $F = f$ on $M_1$, $2a - f$ on $M_2$, is the required round function with at most four singularities.

Proof of Theorem 3.5 (3.5). Suppose an $S^{n-1}$-function $f$ exists on $S^n$; take a value $a$ and its critical sphere $S_1^{n-1}$. By the Jordan--Brouwer theorem, removing a small cylindrical neighbourhood $C_\varepsilon(S_1^{n-1})$ splits $S^n$ into two components $D_1, D_2$ with single boundary components. $D_1$ must contain critical points (else it would be $\partial D_1 \times I$). Removing further critical layers around critical spheres $S_2^{n-1}$, etc., exhausts the finitely many critical submanifolds but leaves a submanifold with a single boundary component containing no critical points, a contradiction.

Proof of Theorem 3.6 (3.6). By Theorem 3.4 (thm:3.4), on $S^3$ there is a round function with two singularities. For $S^4 = D^4/S^3$, split the disc into $N_1, N_2, N_3$ and cover $S^4$ by $M_1 \cong S^1 \times D^3$ and $M_2 \cong S^2 \times D^2$; $M_2$ is covered by two subsets each $\cong S^1 \times D^3$, and with $M_1$ these cover $S^4$, so by Theorem 2.6 (thm:2.5) there is a round function with three critical circles. For $S^5$, cover by $M_1 = S^1 \times D^4$ and $M_2 = S^3 \times D^2$, with $S^3$ (hence $M_2$) covered by two subsets $\cong S^1 \times D^4$, giving by Theorem 2.6 (thm:2.5) a round function with three critical circles. An analogous treatment of higher-dimensional spheres yields the bound $[n/2] + 1$.
